reasoning: Scientific consensus and rigorous double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials have consistently failed to demonstrate a causal link between normal dietary consumption of MSG (monosodium glutamate) and symptoms such as headaches, numbness, or flushing (historically dubbed "Chinese restaurant syndrome"). The term originated from an anecdotal 1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine rather than controlled clinical evidence. Food and health regulatory agencies, including the U.S. FDA, consider MSG to be "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS), noting that the body metabolizes glutamate from MSG identically to glutamate naturally found in foods like tomatoes and aged cheese. While a small subset of individuals may self-report sensitivity, scientific reviews find no reproducible evidence that MSG causes these symptoms.
